topic: Handcuff double lock: ratchet + pawl, the problem (a single-locked cuff can still tighten), the key pin pushes the bolt behind the pawl, the pawl can't lift.
title: Why Handcuffs Have a Double Lock 🔒
principle: The swinging arm carries ratchet teeth; a spring-loaded pawl in the housing rides up the gentle slopes as the arm closes (click) and jams against the steep faces if it is pulled back, so a single-locked cuff can only tighten. Setting the double lock (the pin on the key's end pushes a small bolt) puts the bolt behind the pawl so it cannot lift: the arm can then move neither tighter nor open.
voiceover: Why do handcuffs have a double lock?
Inside, the arm has teeth. A spring pushes a pawl onto them.
Push the arm in. Each tooth lifts the pawl, and it snaps back. Click.
Pull it back, and the steep side of a tooth jams the pawl.
But it can still click tighter, and too tight can hurt the wrist.
So the key's small pin pushes a bolt in, right behind the pawl.
Now the pawl can't lift. It can't get tighter, and it can't open.
The bolt locks the pawl. No more tightening.

firstComment:
Answer: it pushes the double-lock bolt 🔧

Inside the cuff, the swinging arm has a row of ratchet teeth. A spring-loaded pawl presses on them. Push the arm in and each tooth lifts the pawl, which snaps back: click. Pull it back and the steep side of a tooth jams against the pawl, so the cuff can't open without the key.

The catch: a single-locked cuff can still be tightened, even by accident, and overtightened handcuffs can injure the nerves in the wrist.

Double lock: the pin on the end of the key pushes a small bolt in, right behind the pawl. Now the pawl can't lift at all, so the arm can't move either way: no tightening, no opening. To unlock, the key is turned one way to move the bolt back, then the other way to lift the pawl.

(Simplified 3D model, enlarged: one pawl, the front plate removed. Designs vary between brands.)

Sources:
U.S. National Institute of Justice handcuff report, NCJ 86295 (the spring-loaded pawl cams away as the ratchet closes; with the double lock bolt active the pawl cannot cam, so the ratchet can neither close further nor open; to open, the bolt is moved first, then the pawl is lifted): https://www.ojp.gov/pdffiles1/Digitization/86295NCJRS.pdf
US patent 4,509,346 (double locking handcuffs were developed to prevent unwanted further tightening; the bolt is pushed into place by a pin on the end of the handcuff key; the key turns one way to move the bolt, then the other to lift the pawl): https://patents.justia.com/patent/4509346
College of Policing, Handcuffing (double locking prevents further tightening of the ratchets; the tip of the key goes into the double-lock pinhole): https://library.college.police.uk/docs/college-of-policing/PSM_2020/MOD_08_HANDCUFFING-Redacted.pdf
Grant and Cook, Muscle & Nerve 2000, "A prospective study of handcuff neuropathies" (nerve injuries from overtightened handcuffs): https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/10842271
altText: 3D animation explaining the handcuff double lock, with a voiceover. A silver handcuff sits on a forearm under the question Why a double lock? A red circle marks the lock housing. The front plate fades away to show the inside: the curved arm with a row of sawtooth teeth, an orange pawl on a pin, and a coil spring pushing the pawl onto the teeth. Labels name the arm teeth, pawl and spring. 1, an arrow pushes the arm in: each tooth lifts the pawl and it snaps back, CLICK. 2, the arm is pulled back: the steep side of a tooth jams against the pawl, can't open. Then the view pulls back to the wrist: but it can still tighten, two more clicks, the wrist turns red, TOO TIGHT. 3, the pin on the end of a key comes up through a hole in the housing edge and pushes a small blue double-lock bolt in, right behind the pawl. 4, the arm is pushed and pulled again: the pawl can't lift, no tighter, no opening. The payoff text reads Bolt blocks the pawl. No tighter. The front plate returns and a follow line appears before the video loops.
